theory.what: IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6) uses 128-bit addresses (vs IPv4's 32-bit), providing 2^128 (340 undecillion) addresses — enough to assign an IP to every atom on Earth's surface with millions to spare. IPv6 addresses are written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons: 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334. Leading zeros can be omitted, and one contiguous block of zeros can be replaced with '::': 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334. Address types: Global Unicast (2000::/3 — internet-routable, like public IPv4), Unique Local (fc00::/7 — analogous to RFC 1918 private addresses), Link-Local (fe80::/10 — required on every interface, used for neighbor discovery, not routable), Multicast (ff00::/8 — replaces IPv4 broadcast), and Loopback (::1 — equivalent to 127.0.0.1). IPv6 eliminates NAT — every device can have a globally routable address. Autoconfiguration: stateless (SLAAC — router advertises prefix, device generates its interface identifier) or stateful (DHCPv6).
theory.why: IPv6 is essential because the internet has run out of IPv4 addresses — every major mobile network (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile) already runs IPv6-only internally. Key reasons IPv6 matters: (1) IPv4 exhaustion — IANA ran out in 2011, RIRs have run out regionally; (2) No NAT — end-to-end connectivity restored, simplifying peer-to-peer applications, gaming, and VoIP; (3) Simplified addressing — no more subnetting by hand; every network gets a /64 (18 quintillion addresses); (4) Automatic configuration — SLAAC requires no DHCP server; devices self-configure; (5) Better multicast — mandatory, efficient multicast replaces broadcast; (6) Built-in security — IPsec is mandatory in the IPv6 specification; (7) Efficient routing — hierarchical addressing reduces routing table size; (8) Mobile IPv6 built-in — better support for mobile devices moving between networks; (9) Future-proofing — all new internet-connected devices will use IPv6. Global IPv6 adoption is now over 40% and growing. Google, Facebook, Netflix, and Cloudflare all serve content over IPv6. Understanding IPv6 is increasingly required for network engineering roles.
theory.how: IPv6 operation differs significantly from IPv4 in several areas. Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) replaces ARP: Neighbor Solicitation (NS — like ARP Request) and Neighbor Advertisement (NA — like ARP Reply). Router Solicitation (RS) and Router Advertisement (RA) — devices discover routers without DHCP. SLAAC: Routers periodically send Router Advertisements (or respond to RS) containing the prefix (e.g., 2001:db8:1:2::/64). Devices generate their interface identifier from their MAC address using EUI-64 (inserts FFFE in the middle and flips the 7th bit) or use privacy extensions (random temporary addresses). The device combines prefix + identifier = complete IPv6 address. IPv6 header is simpler (40 bytes fixed, no options chaining like IPv4). No checksum at the IP layer (delegated to upper layers for efficiency). No fragmentation by routers (hosts must use Path MTU Discovery). No broadcast (multicast replaces all broadcast functions). DNS: AAAA records (equivalent to IPv4 A records). Transition technologies: Dual-Stack (both IPv4 and IPv6 running simultaneously, most common), Tunnels (6to4, Teredo), and Translation (NAT64/DNS64).
theory.when: IPv6 is already required in: (1) Mobile networks — all major carriers use IPv6-only; (2) Cloud providers — AWS, Azure, GCP all support IPv6; (3) Data centers — Microsoft, Facebook, Google run IPv6 internally; (4) Government networks — US federal government mandated IPv6 support. For enterprise networks: (1) Enable dual-stack on internet-facing services; (2) Configure internal DNS for AAAA records alongside A records; (3) Test IPv6 connectivity to major services; (4) Plan IPv6 addressing scheme for new network builds. Troubleshoot IPv6 when: (1) 'IPv6-enabled' service is unreachable; (2) SLAAC isn't working (devices get link-local only, no global address); (3) DNS AAAA queries fail; (4) IPv6 tunnels misconfigured; (5) Dual-stack applications prefer IPv4 even when IPv6 is available (Happy Eyeballs algorithm issue).
key_concepts: 128-bit address — 8 groups of 4 hex digits, zero compression with ::
Types: Global (2000::/3), Unique Local (fc00::/7), Link-Local (fe80::/10), Multicast (ff00::/8)
SLAAC — Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (no DHCP needed)
NDP — Neighbor Discovery Protocol (replaces ARP + ICMP Router Discovery)
EUI-64 — MAC-to-interface-ID conversion (insert FFFE, flip 7th bit)
No NAT — every device gets a globally routable address
No broadcast — multicast replaces all broadcast functions
Dual-Stack — running both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously (most common transition method)
MSS clamping — TCP MSS adjustment needed at the edge to accommodate the larger IPv6 header
theory.configuration:
# Linux IPv6 configuration
ip -6 addr add 2001:db8::1/64 dev eth0
ip -6 route add default via 2001:db8::ffff

# Cisco IPv6 configuration
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8::1/64
 ipv6 enable  ! Enables link-local address without explicit config

# Enable IPv6 routing
ipv6 unicast-routing
! Router Advertisement (SLAAC)
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8::1/64
 ipv6 nd prefix default  ! Advertise prefix for SLAAC
 ipv6 nd ra-interval 30  ! Router Advertisement every 30 seconds

# Test IPv6
ping6 2001:db8::1
ping -6 2001:db8::1
ping6 -c 4 google.com  # Test via AAAA record

# View IPv6 routing table
ip -6 route show
show ipv6 route

# DNS AAAA record
dig google.com AAAA +short
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Diagnosing 'No IPv6 Connectivity'**
Symptom: ip -6 addr show shows only a link-local address (fe80::), no global (2000::/3) address.

Step 1 — Check router advertisements:
  tcpdump -i eth0 'icmp6 and ip6[40]==134'  # Capture Router Advertisements (type 134)
  If no RAs are received → the router isn't sending them or they're blocked.

Step 2 — On the router, check:
  show ipv6 interface Gi0/0 | include RA
  Is 'Router Advertisement' enabled? Is the router sending RAs?

Step 3 — Check if a global prefix is configured on the router interface:
  show ipv6 interface brief
  If the interface shows only a link-local address, no global prefix is configured.
  Fix: 'ipv6 address 2001:db8:1:1::1/64'

Step 4 — If RAs are sent but not received:
  Check any switches between the client and router — RA packets are multicast and must traverse the switch.
  Check if MLD snooping is filtering the RA multicast group.

**Worked Example 2: Dual-Stack Operation**
A server with both IPv4 (192.168.1.10) and IPv6 (2001:db8:1:1::10) addresses.

nslookup myserver.example.com
  Name: myserver.example.com
  Addresses: 2001:db8:1:1::10  (AAAA record)
             192.168.1.10        (A record)

Client's Happy Eyeballs algorithm tries both addresses and uses whichever connects first (typically IPv6 if available).

If the server is unreachable over IPv6 but reachable over IPv4:
- Check firewall rules for IPv6 traffic
- Check if the router has a default IPv6 route
- Check DNS AAAA record is correct

The client should automatically fall back to IPv4 after a brief delay.

**Worked Example 3: IPv6 Tunnel Broker**
If your ISP doesn't natively support IPv6, you can use a tunnel broker (Hurricane Electric, SixXS) to tunnel IPv6 over IPv4.

Cisco IPv6 manual tunnel:
  interface Tunnel0
   tunnel source 203.0.113.1
   tunnel destination 216.66.80.30  ! HE tunnel server
   tunnel mode ipv6ip
   ipv6 address 2001:470:1f10:2::2/64
   ipv6 enable

Test: ping6 2001:470:0:9c::2 (HE test address). If it works, IPv6 over tunnel is operational.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (8 groups of 4 hex digits) with zero compression (::)
• Address types: Global (2000::/3), Unique Local (fc00::/7), Link-Local (fe80::/10), Multicast (ff00::/8)
• SLAAC enables stateless autoconfiguration without DHCP
• NDP replaces ARP with Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement messages
• No NAT, No broadcast, No router fragmentation
• Dual-Stack is the most common transition method (both v4 and v6)

**Best Practice:** Enable dual-stack on all infrastructure. Plan your IPv6 addressing scheme (/64 per subnet, /48 per site). Use privacy extensions for client devices. Test connectivity with ping6 before assuming IPv6 works.
troubleshooting: ping6 <dst> — test IPv6 connectivity
ip -6 addr show — view IPv6 addresses on interfaces
ip -6 route show — view IPv6 routing table
show ipv6 interface brief — Cisco interface IPv6 status
ping6 google.com — test end-to-end IPv6 connectivity (requires AAAA DNS)
dig google.com AAAA — check DNS AAAA records
tcpdump -i eth0 icmp6 — capture IPv6 ICMP (NDP, RA, NS/NA)
Check firewall rules for IPv6 traffic (many firewalls have separate IPv6 rulesets!)
If IPv6 works for some sites but not others → DNS/connectivity issue for specific destinations
Check for IPv6 tunnel if ISP doesn't natively support IPv6

theory.what: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the foundation of data communication on the World Wide Web, operating at Layer 7 (Application) of the OSI model. HTTP follows a request-response model: a client (browser, curl, API consumer) sends an HTTP request to a server, which processes it and returns an HTTP response. HTTP was designed as a simple, human-readable text-based protocol over TCP. HTTPS (HTTP Secure) adds TLS encryption over TCP port 443, providing confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication. The protocol has evolved through versions: HTTP/0.9 (simple GET requests only), HTTP/1.0 (headers, status codes), HTTP/1.1 (persistent connections, chunked transfer, host header — still the most common version), HTTP/2 (multiplexed streams, header compression, server push), and HTTP/3 (over QUIC/UDP for reduced latency). Each HTTP request consists of: a request line (METHOD path HTTP/version), headers (key-value pairs), and an optional body. Each HTTP response has: a status line (HTTP/version status-code reason-phrase), headers, and an optional body.
theory.why: HTTP/HTTPS is the most important application protocol in modern networking — virtually every service, API, and website uses it. Understanding HTTP is essential for: (1) Web debugging — browser developer tools reveal HTTP request/response details; (2) API integration — REST APIs use HTTP methods as verbs (GET=read, POST=create, PUT=update, DELETE=remove); (3) Security analysis — HTTPS certificate validation, HSTS, CORS, CSP all rely on HTTP mechanisms; (4) Performance optimization — understanding caching headers, compression, keep-alive, and pipelining; (5) Troubleshooting — HTTP status codes give precise error information: 4xx means client error, 5xx means server error; (6) Load balancing — ALBs, reverse proxies, and CDNs operate at the HTTP layer; (7) Web application firewalls (WAF) — inspect and filter HTTP traffic for attacks. A network engineer who understands HTTP can diagnose problems that look like 'network issues' but are actually application-layer problems.
theory.how:
HTTP request structure: A client sends 'GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
User-Agent: curl/8.0
Accept: */*

'. The server responds: 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1234
Cache-Control: max-age=3600

<html>...'. HTTP Methods: GET (retrieve resource, no body), POST (submit data to create/process), PUT (replace/update resource), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove resource), HEAD (like GET but no body), OPTIONS (available methods), TRACE (diagnostic loopback). HTTP Status Code Groups: 1xx (Informational — 101 Switching Protocols for WebSocket upgrade), 2xx (Success — 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx (Redirection — 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified for caching), 4xx (Client Error — 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 408 Request Timeout, 429 Too Many Requests), 5xx (Server Error — 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout). HTTPS adds TLS: Client sends ClientHello (supported cipher suites, TLS version) → Server responds with ServerHello (chosen cipher, certificate) → Certificate verification → Key exchange → Encrypted data transfer.
theory.when: Use HTTP/HTTPS knowledge for: (1) API debugging — curl -v https://api.example.com; (2) Certificate troubleshooting — openssl s_client -connect example.com:443; (3) Performance analysis — check response times, caching headers, compression; (4) Security testing — verify HTTPS is properly configured; (5) Redirect chain analysis — track 301/302 to final destination; (6) Content negotiation — Accept headers for different response formats; (7) Authentication debugging — check 401/403 responses for auth failures. Troubleshoot HTTP when: (1) Site fails to load but ping works → probably not a network issue; (2) 404 errors → wrong URL or resource path; (3) 500 errors → server problem, not network; (4) 301/302 redirect loops → misconfigured web server; (5) Mixed content warnings (HTTP + HTTPS on same page) to update links; (6) SSL/TLS errors → certificate expired, mismatched hostname, or protocol version issues.
key_concepts: Request/Response model — client sends request, server returns response
Methods — GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (update), DELETE (remove)
Status codes — 2xx (success), 3xx (redirect), 4xx (client error), 5xx (server error)
HTTPS = HTTP + TLS (encryption + certificate verification)
Headers — metadata in requests (Cookies, Authorization) and responses (Set-Cookie, Cache-Control)
HTTP/1.1 — persistent connections, host header, chunked transfer encoding
HTTP/2 — multiplexed streams over single TCP connection, header compression (HPACK)
HTTP/3 — over QUIC (UDP), solving TCP head-of-line blocking
Caching — ETag, Last-Modified, Cache-Control for efficient resource reuse
CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, browser security mechanism
REST — Representational State Transfer, architectural style using HTTP methods as verbs
theory.configuration:
# Basic HTTP request
curl -v http://example.com

# Show only response headers
curl -I https://example.com

# POST request with JSON body
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/data \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"test","value":42}'

# Test HTTPS certificate
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com

# Follow redirects
curl -L http://bitly.is/shorturl

# Custom headers

# HTTP/2 test

# Test IPv4 vs IPv6

curl -6 https://example.com
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Diagnosing 'Site Not Loading'**
A user reports a website won't load. Ping to the host works (IP reachable).

Step 1 — Check HTTP status with curl:
  curl -v https://example.com

Step 2 — Interpret the response:
  - If curl succeeds (200 OK) → server is responding, problem is browser-side (cache, proxy, extension)
  - If curl gets Connection refused (curl: (7)) → nothing listening on port 80/443
  - If curl gets timeout (curl: (28)) → firewall blocking or server too busy
  - If curl gets 500 error → server application problem
  - If curl gets 301/302 → check redirect target, might be a redirect loop

Step 3 — If Connection refused:
  Check if the web server is running: 'systemctl status nginx' or 'ss -tlnp | grep 443'
  Check if the firewall allows port 443: 'iptables -L -n | grep 443'

**Worked Example 2: Certificate Validation Failure**
Symptom: Browser shows 'Your connection is not private.'

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'error|return|verify'

Common certificate errors:
1. Certificate expired: 'verify error:num=10:certificate has expired'
   → Renew the certificate with the CA
2. Hostname mismatch: 'SSL: certificate subject name 'wrong.com' does not match host name 'example.com''
   → Get a certificate for the correct domain or fix the DNS
3. Self-signed certificate: 'verify error:num=18:self-signed certificate'
   → For internal use only; add to trust store or get a proper CA-signed cert
4. Chain incomplete: 'verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate'
   → Install the intermediate certificate on the server

**Worked Example 3: Redirect Chain Analysis**
A site redirects multiple times before loading, causing slow performance.

curl -IL https://example.com

Output showing the redirect chain:
  HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently → https://www.example.com
  HTTP/1.1 302 Found → https://www.example.com/en/
  HTTP/1.1 200 OK → Final page

Each redirect adds an extra round-trip (and TLS handshake if going HTTP→HTTPS). Optimize by:
1. Reducing redirects — directly configure the destination
2. Adding HSTS header to prevent HTTP→HTTPS redirect on subsequent visits
3. Using 301 (cached by browser) instead of 302 (not cached) for permanent redirects
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• HTTP is a text-based request-response protocol at Layer 7, the foundation of web communication
• HTTPS adds TLS encryption (port 443), providing confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication
• Status codes: 2xx=success, 3xx=redirect, 4xx=client error, 5xx=server error
• curl -v is the most versatile HTTP troubleshooting tool
• HTTP methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), DELETE (remove)
• HTTP/2 multiplexes requests; HTTP/3 uses QUIC/UDP for reduced latency

**Best Practice:** Use curl -v for detailed request/response debugging. Verify HTTPS with openssl s_client. Monitor HTTP status codes in application logs (4xx=user issues, 5xx=server issues). Use browser dev tools Network tab for complete request timelines.
troubleshooting: curl -v http://example.com — verbose output with request/response details
curl -I http://example.com — head request (response headers only)
curl -L http://shorturl — follow redirect chain
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 — test TLS connection, view certificate
curl -o /dev/null -s -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com — only show status code

curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'Connect: %{time_connect}s
TTFB: %{time_starttransfer}s
Total: %{time_total}s
' https://example.com — connection timing
Check browser Developer Tools → Network tab: status codes, timing, headers
HTTP 404 → resource not found; 403 → forbidden; 401 → unauthorized; 500 → server crash
HTTPS errors → check certificate expiry, hostname match, intermediate chain

theory.what: SSH (Secure Shell) is a cryptographic network protocol for secure remote access, command execution, and file transfer over an insecure network. It replaces insecure protocols like Telnet (plaintext, sends passwords in the clear), rsh, and rlogin. SSH provides: strong encryption (all traffic is encrypted), integrity verification (data can't be modified in transit), and authentication (server proves its identity via host keys; clients authenticate via passwords or public keys). SSH operates on TCP port 22 by default. The protocol has two major versions: SSH-1 (deprecated, insecure) and SSH-2 (current standard, defined in RFC 4251-4256). SSH-2 supports multiple authentication methods (public key, password, keyboard-interactive, GSSAPI), port forwarding (local, remote, dynamic), X11 forwarding (GUI apps over SSH), and SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol). The SSH client configuration file (~/.ssh/config) allows per-host settings that significantly simplify daily use.
theory.why: SSH is the standard method for managing virtually all Linux servers, network devices (routers, switches, firewalls), and cloud infrastructure. Understanding SSH is essential for: (1) Secure remote administration — every server and network device is managed via SSH; (2) Public key authentication — more secure than passwords, enables automation; (3) File transfer — SCP and SFTP are the standard secure file transfer methods; (4) Port forwarding/tunneling — SSH can forward local ports to remote services through firewalls; (5) Jump hosts/bastion hosts — SSH through a bastion to reach private subnets; (6) Automation — SSH keys enable passwordless authentication for scripts, Ansible, and CI/CD systems; (7) Git — Git over SSH (git@github.com:user/repo.git) is the standard for developers. A network engineer who doesn't understand SSH keys, agent forwarding, and config files will struggle with device automation and server management.
theory.how: SSH connection establishment follows this process. Phase 1 — TCP Connection: Client connects to server on TCP port 22. Phase 2 — Protocol Version Exchange: Client and server agree on SSH version (typically 2.0). Phase 3 — Key Exchange (Diffie-Hellman): Both sides generate ephemeral key pairs, exchange public keys, and compute a shared secret. This Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) ensures that even if the server's long-term private key is compromised, past sessions cannot be decrypted. Phase 4 — Server Authentication: The server sends its host key (RSA, ECDSA, or Ed25519). The client checks if the host key is known (stored in ~/.ssh/known_hosts). If unknown, the client warns the user. Phase 5 — Client Authentication: Password (sent over encrypted channel), public key (sign a challenge), or keyboard-interactive. Phase 6 — Encrypted Session: An encrypted channel is established for data transfer. Features: Port Forwarding (-L, -R, -D), Agent Forwarding (-A), X11 Forwarding (-X), Compression (-C), and Connection Sharing (ControlMaster for multiplexing multiple sessions over one TCP connection).
theory.when: Use SSH for: (1) Remote server management — ssh user@server; (2) File transfer — scp, sftp, rsync over SSH; (3) Port forwarding — access services on a remote network through a tunnel; (4) Tunneling through firewalls — use SSH as a SOCKS proxy (-D); (5) Connecting to cloud instances — AWS EC2, Azure VMs, GCP instances all use SSH key authentication; (6) Network device management — routers, switches, firewalls; (7) Git operations — git push/pull over SSH. Troubleshoot SSH when: (1) Connection refused — SSH server not running; (2) Permission denied — wrong credentials; (3) Host key verification failed — server's host key changed; (4) Connection timed out — firewall blocking port 22; (5) 'Too many authentication failures' — too many keys offered; (6) 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED' — host key mismatch (potential MITM attack or server reinstall).
key_concepts: Port 22 (TCP) — default SSH port; change for security (optional)
Public key authentication — client generates key pair, sends public key to server
Host key verification — server proves identity; stored in ~/.ssh/known_hosts
SSH config file (~/.ssh/config) — per-host configuration (alias, keys, options)
Port forwarding — -L (local), -R (remote), -D (dynamic/SOCKS proxy)
Agent forwarding (-A) — use local SSH keys through a jump host (be careful: forward to trusted hosts only!)
SCP/SFTP — file transfer over SSH
Permissons: ~/.ssh = 700, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys = 600, private keys = 600
Ed25519 — recommended key type (short, fast, secure)
jump host / bastion — SSH through an intermediary to reach private networks
theory.configuration:
# Generate SSH key (Ed25519 recommended)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "user@hostname" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# Copy public key to server
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@server
# Or manually
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | ssh user@server "mkdir -p ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"

# SSH config (~/.ssh/config) — simplifies connections
Host webserver
  HostName 192.168.1.10
  User admin
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  Port 2222  # Non-standard port

Host bastion
  HostName bastion.example.com
  User jumpuser
  ForwardAgent yes

Host internal-*
  User appuser
  ProxyJump bastion  # Through bastion
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# Port forwarding examples
ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 user@server  # Local port 8080 → remote server's port 80
ssh -R 9090:localhost:9090 user@server  # Remote port 9090 → local port 9090
ssh -D 1080 user@server  # SOCKS proxy on local port 1080

# Verbose debugging
ssh -vvv user@server
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: SSH Connection Refused**
Symptom: ssh user@server returns 'Connection refused'.

Step 1 — Check if SSH server is running:
  systemctl status sshd  # or 'sudo service sshd status'
  If not running: sudo systemctl start sshd && sudo systemctl enable sshd

Step 2 — Check if port 22 is listening:
  ss -tlnp | grep 22  (netstat -tlnp | grep 22)
  If not listening → SSH daemon crashed or not started

Step 3 — Check firewall:
  sudo iptables -L -n | grep 22
  sudo firewall-cmd --list-all | grep 22
  If blocked: sudo ufw allow 22/tcp or add iptables/firewalld rule

Step 4 — Test locally first:
  ssh localhost  # Test if SSH works on the server itself
  If local works but remote doesn't → firewall blocking

**Worked Example 2: SSH Key Permission Denied**
Symptom: Permission denied (publickey) but key was added to authorized_keys.

Step 1 — Check permissions on server:
  ls -la ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
  Permissions must be 600 (-rw-------)!
  Fix: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Step 2 — Check home directory and .ssh permissions:
  ls -ld ~/ → must NOT be writable by group or other (755 or 700)
  ls -ld ~/.ssh → must be 700 (drwx------)
  Fix: chmod 700 ~/.ssh ; chmod 755 ~  (if home is 755)

Step 3 — Check server logs:
  sudo tail -f /var/log/auth.log  # Debian/Ubuntu
  sudo tail -f /var/log/secure   # RHEL/CentOS
  Look for: 'Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes' or 'Failed publickey'

Step 4 — SSH config (/etc/ssh/sshd_config):
  Verify: PubkeyAuthentication yes
  Verify: AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys

**Worked Example 3: SSH Tunneling to Reach a Private Database**
Architecture: Your local machine → Bastion host (public IP) → Private RDS database (private IP 10.0.0.50:3306)

Local port forwarding through bastion:
  ssh -L 3306:10.0.0.50:3306 user@bastion.example.com -N
  # -N: don't open a shell, just forward ports

Now connect to localhost:3306 on your machine, and it tunnel through the bastion to the private database.

Using SSH config:
  Host dbtunnel
    HostName bastion.example.com
    User jumpuser
    LocalForward 3306 10.0.0.50:3306
  
  ssh dbtunnel -N
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• SSH provides encrypted remote access (port 22), replacing Telnet and rsh
• Public key authentication is more secure than passwords and enables automation
• Permission requirements: ~/.ssh = 700, authorized_keys = 600, private keys = 600
• SSH config file (~/.ssh/config) simplifies connections with per-host settings
• Port forwarding (-L, -R, -D) creates encrypted tunnels through firewalls
• ProxyJump simplifies multi-hop SSH connections
• Ed25519 is the recommended key type (fast, secure, short keys)

**Best Practice:** Use Ed25519 keys. Disable password authentication in production (PasswordAuthentication no). Use SSH config files for organization. Use ProxyJump for bastion hosts. Never use SSH-1 (deprecated). Monitor auth.log for failed login attempts.
troubleshooting: ssh -vvv user@host — verbose debugging (v=protocol, vv=detailed, vvv=debug)
ss -tlnp | grep 22 — verify sshd is listening
systemctl status sshd — check SSH server status
tail -f /var/log/auth.log — check authentication logs
Check permissions: ~/.ssh must be 700, authorized_keys must be 600
Connection refused → SSH server not running or firewall blocking port 22
Permission denied → wrong credentials, wrong key, or bad permissions
Host key changed → server reinstalled; remove old key from ~/.ssh/known_hosts
scp -v / scp -vvv for file transfer debugging

theory.what: FTP (File Transfer Protocol, RFC 959) transfers files over a network using a client-server architecture. It uses separate control (TCP port 21) and data connections. FTP supports active mode (server connects to client's data port) and passive mode (client connects to server's data port). Passive mode is typically required through firewalls and NAT. FTP is inherently insecure: all traffic including passwords is sent in plaintext. SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) is entirely different from FTP — it's a file transfer protocol that runs over the SSH protocol (port 22), providing encryption, authentication, and integrity. SFTP supports directory listing, file deletion, resume, and permission management. SCP (Secure Copy) is the simplest form: file copying over SSH (port 22), with no interactive file management. FTPS (FTP over TLS) adds TLS encryption to traditional FTP, using ports 990 (control) and sometimes 989 (data). Despite FTP's age and security issues, it's still encountered in legacy systems, industrial equipment, and some web hosting environments.
theory.why: Understanding the differences between file transfer protocols is critical for security: (1) FTP sends passwords in plaintext — anyone on the network can capture them with tcpdump; (2) FTP active mode doesn't work through NAT without ALG support; (3) FTP is still commonly found in embedded systems and legacy equipment; (4) SFTP/SCP should always be preferred for any file transfer involving sensitive data; (5) Passive FTP issues are a common troubleshooting scenario; (6) SFTP provides interactive file management (browse, delete, rename) that SCP doesn't. For network engineers, knowing when to use each protocol and how to troubleshoot passive FTP issues is an important skill.
theory.how: FTP Active Mode: Client connects to server's port 21 (control). Client sends PORT command with its IP and port. Server connects to client's data port: Client's port 20 (server) → Client's data port (client). Problem: The server initiates the data connection to the client, which NAT/firewalls typically block. FTP Passive Mode: Client connects to server's port 21 (control). Client sends PASV command. Server responds with its IP and port. Client connects to server's data port from a random client port. Advantage: Client initiates both connections, works through NAT. Disadvantage: Server must be configured with a range of passive ports, and these must be open in the firewall. SFTP: Operates over SSH (port 22). All traffic encrypted. Commands include: ls, cd, get, put, rm, mkdir, chmod. No separate data connection — everything over the SSH channel. SCP: scp [-r] source destination. Copies files over SSH. Simple, no interactive mode. FTPS: Like FTP but wrapped in TLS. Explicit FTPS (AUTH TLS): Client connects to port 21, upgrades to TLS. Implicit FTPS: Client connects to port 990, TLS established immediately.
theory.when: Use SFTP for all file transfers requiring: (1) security — passwords and data encrypted; (2) interactive management — browse, delete, rename, chmod; (3) resume — partial transfer can be resumed; (4) scriptability — sftp -b batchfile. Use SCP for simple single-file copying. Use FTP only with legacy systems that don't support SFTP/SCP — and only over isolated/trusted networks. Use FTPS when forced to use FTP but need encryption. Troubleshoot FTP when: (1) FTP connects but directory listing times out — passive mode issue; (2) File transfer fails after login — active mode blocked by firewall; (3) '425 Can't open data connection' — the classic FTP firewall/NAT problem; (4) SFTP 'Expected SSH_FXP_INIT' — trying to SFTP to a server that only supports FTP. Network security best practice: Block FTP (port 21) at the firewall. Require SFTP/SCP for all file transfers.
key_concepts: FTP — plaintext, two ports (21 control, variable data), insecure
Active mode — server connects to client's data port (blocked by NAT)
Passive mode (PASV) — client connects to server's data port (recommended, works through NAT)
SFTP — file transfer over SSH (port 22), encrypted, interactive
SCP — secure copy over SSH (port 22), simple non-interactive copy
FTPS — FTP with TLS (ports 990 implicit, 21 explicit)
Passive port range — configurable range of data ports on the server (e.g., 30000-31000)
Binary vs ASCII mode — binary preserves exact file; ASCII converts line endings
Anonymous FTP — no authentication required (high security risk, avoid)
theory.configuration:
# SCP (simplest — copy files)
scp file.txt user@server:/path/
scp -r directory/ user@server:/path/
scp user@server:/remote/file.txt ./

# SFTP (interactive)
sftp user@server
sftp> ls
sftp> cd /remote/path
sftp> put localfile.txt
sftp> put -r localdir/  # recursive
sftp> get remotefile.txt
sftp> get -r remotedir/

# FTP (legacy, avoid)
ftp server.example.com  # Log in with username/password (insecure!)
ftp> passive  # Toggle passive mode
ftp> binary   # Binary transfer mode
ftp> get file.txt

# Linux FTP server (vsftpd)
sudo apt install vsftpd
sudo systemctl enable vsftpd
# vsftpd.conf:
anonymous_enable=NO
local_enable=YES
write_enable=YES
pasv_enable=YES
pasv_min_port=30000
pasv_max_port=31000
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Passive FTP Not Working Behind Firewall**
Symptom: FTP connects successfully (port 21), login works, but directory listing times out.

Root cause: The client sent PASV command, server responded with its own private IP (e.g., 10.0.0.50:30001) instead of its public IP. The client tries to connect to 10.0.0.50:30001 which isn't reachable.

Fix 1 — Configure the FTP server to report the public IP:
  pasv_address=203.0.113.50  # Server's public IP
  pasv_enable=YES
  pasv_min_port=30000
  pasv_max_port=31000

Fix 2 — Open the passive port range in the firewall:
  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 30000:31000 -j ACCEPT

Fix 3 — Test with explicit passive:
  ftp> passive  # Toggle passive mode
  ftp> ls

**Worked Example 2: Choosing SFTP over FTP**
An organization needs to automate daily file transfers between servers. Currently using FTP.

Security assessment:
- FTP sends password in plaintext → anyone on the network can capture it
- FTP data sent in plaintext → files can be read in transit
- PCI DSS requirement: data must be encrypted in transit → FTP fails

Migration to SFTP:
1. Install SSH server if not already present (usually is)
2. Generate SSH key: ssh-keygen -t ed25519
3. Add public key to target server's authorized_keys
4. Test: sftp user@server
5. Create script: sftp -b batchfile.txt user@server
6. Verify: run the script and check file integrity

**Worked Example 3: Diagnosing SCP Failures**
Symptom: scp file.txt user@server:/path/ fails with 'Permission denied'.

Step 1 — Check SSH access first:
  ssh user@server ls /path/
  If SSH works, the problem is SCP-specific.

Step 2 — Check SCP binary location:
  On the server: which scp
  If not found: 'sudo apt install openssh-client' or equivalent

Step 3 — Check SSH config:
  /etc/ssh/sshd_config: Subsystem sftp /usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server
  (SFTP subsystem is required; SCP may or may not use it)

Step 4 — Check write permissions on target directory:
  ssh user@server ls -ld /path/
  User must have write permission on the directory.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• FTP is insecure (plaintext passwords/data) — use SFTP/SCP instead
• FTP Active Mode doesn't work through NAT — use Passive Mode with configured port range
• SFTP runs over SSH (port 22) with full encryption and interactive file management
• SCP is the simplest file copy over SSH (non-interactive)
• FTPS adds TLS to FTP (ports 990 implicit, 21 explicit)
• Passive FTP troubleshooting: check PASV address, port range, and firewall rules

**Best Practice:** Never use plain FTP for sensitive data. Use SFTP or SCP for all file transfers. Block FTP (port 21) at the firewall and only allow SFTP/SCP (port 22). For legacy FTP-only systems, use FTPS if available or accept the security risk on isolated networks.
troubleshooting: Check port connectivity: nc -zv server 22 (SFTP) vs nc -zv server 21 (FTP)
FTP passive mode fails: configure pasv_address and pasv port range on server
SCP fails: verify SSH access first, check target directory permissions
SFTP hangs: check if server is actually running SSH (might be pure FTP server)
FTP directory listing hangs: classic passive mode issue
FTP in NAT: configure FTP ALG on firewall (often adds problems, prefer passive mode)
File integrity issue: always use binary mode (not ASCII) for non-text files
Check file permissions: ls -la target/ to verify write access

theory.what: Network Time Protocol (NTP, RFC 5905) synchronizes clocks across computer systems and network devices over packet-switched networks. NTP uses a hierarchical system of time sources and can achieve accuracy within milliseconds over the public internet and microseconds on local networks. The hierarchy uses Stratum levels: Stratum 0 (atomic clocks, GPS receivers — the high-precision reference clocks), Stratum 1 (servers directly connected to Stratum 0, like pool.ntp.org's tier-1 servers), Stratum 2 (servers synchronized to Stratum 1), and so on. Each level introduces slightly more inaccuracy. NTP operates over UDP port 123. It uses a sophisticated algorithm to select the best time source, filter out outliers, and adjust the clock gradually (slew) rather than instantly jumping — preventing discontinuities in logs and timestamps. NTP can also authenticate time sources using symmetric keys for security. On modern Linux systems, chronyd has largely replaced the older ntpd daemon, offering faster synchronization and better handling of network interruptions.
theory.why: Accurate time synchronization is critically important for network operations and security. Without NTP: (1) Logs are useless for incident response — correlating events across devices requires synchronized timestamps; (2) Kerberos authentication fails — it requires time within 5 minutes of the KDC; (3) TLS/SSL certificates appear expired or not-yet-valid if device clocks are wrong; (4) Certificate revocation lists (CRL) fail verification; (5) DNS zone transfers fail — DNS serial numbers rely on accurate timestamps; (6) SIEM/SOC operations impossible — correlating events from different sources requires synchronized time; (7) Compliance requirements (PCI DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA) mandate accurate time synchronization; (8) Scheduled tasks (backups, cron jobs, maintenance windows) execute at wrong times; (9) Forensic analysis requires accurate timeline reconstruction. In cybersecurity, the most common phrase during incident response is 'We need to check the logs' — but if those logs have different clocks, the timeline is corrupted.
theory.how: NTP synchronisation follows this process. The client sends an NTP request (UDP port 123) to the server, including its current timestamp (T1). The server receives the request at T2, sends a response at T3 including T1, T2, T3, and the server's reference timestamp. The client receives the response at T4. From these four timestamps, the client calculates: round-trip delay = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2), and time offset = ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2. The client uses multiple time sources (typically 4+ servers), employing algorithms to detect and discard faulty servers (false tickers), filter outliers, and select the best time source. The clock is then adjusted gradually (slew) — if the difference is small (< 128ms typical), NTP slews the clock (adjusts by a few milliseconds per second); if the difference is large (> 128ms), NTP steps the clock (jumps). On chrony systems, the initial sync is a 'step' followed by 'slew' adjustments to maintain accuracy. NTP queries servers periodically (poll interval typically 64-1024 seconds, doubling until stable). Stratum levels determine clock quality: lower stratum = more accurate. An NTP server should use multiple upstream servers (at least 4) and multiple reference clocks for redundancy.
theory.when: Configure NTP on EVERY network device and server. Specific use cases: (1) All network infrastructure — routers, switches, firewalls, load balancers; (2) All servers — domain controllers, mail servers, web servers, database servers; (3) Security appliances — SIEM, IDS/IPS, firewalls; (4) Storage systems — SAN/NAS; (5) Virtualization hosts — Hyper-V, VMware ESXi; (6) All Linux/Windows systems. Troubleshoot NTP when: (1) Kerberos authentication fails — 'KRB5KDC_ERR_SKEW' means time difference > 5 minutes; (2) Certificate warnings — devices think certs are expired; (3) Logs have wrong timestamps — NTP not configured or drifing; (4) Users report wrong file timestamps; (5) Scheduled tasks run at wrong times; (6) Database replication conflicts — due to timestamp ordering issues. Always use at least two NTP sources for redundancy. For time-sensitive environments, consider GPS-based NTP appliances for stratum-1 accuracy.
key_concepts: Stratum — hierarchical level (0=reference clock, 1=connected to reference, 2=synced to 1, etc.)
NTP client — sends periodic queries to NTP servers (UDP 123)
NTP server — responds with its current time
Chrony — modern Linux NTP implementation (faster, better with intermittent connections)
Clock slew — gradual adjustment (small diff); Clock step — instant adjustment (large diff)
Symmetric key authentication — NTP messages can be authenticated to prevent attacks
Pool.ntp.org — global NTP pool (free, redundant, recommended for general use)
Stratum 0 — reference clocks: GPS, atomic clocks, radio clocks
Monlist (deprecated) — legacy NTP query that was used in DDoS amplification attacks
theory.configuration:
# Cisco NTP configuration
ntp server 0.pool.ntp.org
ntp server 1.pool.ntp.org
ntp server 10.0.0.5  # Internal NTP server
ntp source Loopback0  # Use loopback for consistent source IP
ntp update-calendar  # Update hardware clock

# Verify NTP on Cisco
show ntp status
show ntp associations

# Linux Chrony configuration (/etc/chrony/chrony.conf)
pool 0.pool.ntp.org iburst
pool 1.pool.ntp.org iburst
pool 2.pool.ntp.org iburst
# Allow clients from local network
allow 192.168.0.0/16
# Local stratum if upstream unavailable
local stratum 10

# Chrony commands
chronyc sources -v    # Show NTP sources and their status
chronyc tracking      # Show current time synchronization status
chronyc activity      # Show how many sources are online/offline

# Manual time synchronization
sudo ntpdate -u 0.pool.ntp.org  # One-time sync (legacy, use chronyd instead)

# Linux client quick test
ntpq -p  # Show NTP peers (requires ntp or ntpdate installed)
chronyc tracking | grep -E 'System time|Stratum'
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Diagnosing 'No Time Sync'**
Symptom: chronyc sources shows servers with '?' status (no response).

Step 1 — Check network connectivity to NTP servers:
  chronyc sources -v
  '^?' means unreachable. '^*' means current sync source.

Step 2 — Firewall check:
  Is UDP port 123 allowed outbound? Use tcpdump -i eth0 'port 123' and look for packets.
  Is UDP port 123 open on the firewall? Check iptables/nftables rules.

Step 3 — DNS resolution:
  Can the ntp server hostname be resolved? nslookup 0.pool.ntp.org

Step 4 — Verify chronyd is running:
  systemctl status chronyd
  sudo systemctl restart chronyd

Step 5 — Manual test:
  chronyd -q 'pool 0.pool.ntp.org iburst'  (one-time sync attempt)

**Worked Example 2: NTP with Authentication**
Prevent NTP clients from being tricked into using a rogue time server.

On NTP server:
  /etc/chrony/chrony.conf:
    keyfile /etc/chrony/chrony.keys
    ntpkey NTPkey
    authselectmode require
  
Create key:
  chronyc keygen 1 SHA256 >> /etc/chrony/chrony.keys

On NTP client:
  server ntp-server.example.com key 1

This ensures the client only accepts time updates from a server that knows the shared key.

**Worked Example 3: Setting Up a Local NTP Server**
For an isolated network (no internet), set up a local NTP server:

Server config (/etc/chrony/chrony.conf):
  server 127.127.1.0  # Local clock (fallback)
  local stratum 10    # Declare local as time source
  allow 192.168.0.0/16
  # If a GPS receiver is available:
  refclock SHM 0 offset 0.0 delay 0.2 refid GPS

Client config:
  pool 192.168.1.10 iburst  # Internal NTP server

Without GPS: All devices will show the same time, but it will drift relative to real time. This is acceptable for many internal applications (log correlation, Kerberos) where all devices agree, even if they're slightly wrong.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• NTP synchronizes clocks across devices using a hierarchical Stratum system
• Stratum 0 = reference clocks (GPS, atomic); higher strata = further from reference
• NTP uses UDP port 123 and four-timestamp algorithm (T1-T4) for precise synchronization
• Chrony is the modern NTP implementation (faster, better with network interruptions)
• Accurate time is critical for: log correlation, Kerberos auth, certificate validation, and compliance
• Use at least 2-4 NTP sources for reliability; use the ntp.org pool for public reference

**Best Practice:** Configure NTP on EVERY network device during initial setup. Use chronyd on Linux (not ntpd). Point internal devices to your own NTP servers (not directly to internet pools) for better security and reduced external dependency. Monitor synchronization status regularly.
troubleshooting: show ntp status (Cisco) — check time sync status, stratum, reference
show ntp associations (Cisco) — view NTP server details and reachability
chronyc sources -v (Linux) — view NTP sources with status indicators
chronyc tracking (Linux) — current sync status, offset, stratum
chronyc activity (Linux) — source connectivity status
ntpq -p (Linux) — legacy NTP query tool
Check UDP 123 outbound connectivity to NTP servers
Large offset (> 1s): DNS or DHCP misconfiguration? Check timezone settings.
No sync: Check firewall, DNS resolution, and chronyd service status
Clock jumps: Check for duplicate NTP services running, or manual time changes
